content: The definition of multivessel disease (MVD) for the AEGIS-II inclusion criteria 5 can be established based on findings from cardiac catheterization performed during the index myocardial infarction (MI), findings from a prior cardiac catheterization, or a combination of both. The specific criteria are as follows: 1. Index MI Cardiac Catheterization: Multivessel disease is defined as the presence of 50% or greater stenosis in the left main coronary artery or in at least two coronary artery territories, which include the left anterior descending (LAD), left circumflex (LCx), and right coronary artery (RCA). This assessment must be made prior to any interventional procedures being performed. 2. Prior Cardiac Catheterization: Multivessel disease is similarly defined as 50% or greater stenosis in the left main coronary artery or in at least two coronary artery territories (LAD, LCx, RCA), as determined from a previous cardiac catheterization. Again, this determination must be made before any interventions were performed. 3. Combination of Both: Multivessel disease can also be identified if the index MI cardiac catheterization reveals at least one vessel with 50% or greater stenosis (prior to any interventions) and there is evidence of a prior percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) involving at least one vessel that is different from the vessel identified during the index MI. 4. Prior Multivessel Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG): A history of multivessel CABG also qualifies as evidence of multivessel disease. For the purposes of defining multivessel disease, there must be 50% or greater stenosis in at least two of the three major epicardial coronary artery territories (LAD, LCx, RCA) or in the left main coronary artery. Branch vessels may also be considered as part of the territory of their parent vessel. For example, a diagonal branch is considered part of the LAD territory, and the ramus intermedius is considered part of the LCx territory. If a branch vessel is used to meet the criteria for multivessel disease, the branch must be of sufficient size to be a candidate for revascularization if clinically indicated, typically defined as a vessel with a diameter greater than 2 mm.
